title: Heroes in the Landscape
subtitle: Constellations, city names, and seas — myth written on the world

learningObjectives.text: Which heroes are in the night sky?

main.work: Studies in Greek Scenery, Legend and History
main.author: James George Frazer
main.locator: Frazer's discussion of Pausanias and Mount Sipylus; local text, normalized characters 21213-21905
main.excerpt: This is nearly a direct affirmation that the region about Mount Sipylus in Lydia was his native land. The same thing appears, though less directly, from the minute acquaintance he displays with the district and from the evident fondness with which he recurs again and again to its scenery and legends. He had seen the white eagles wheeling above the lonely tarn of Tantalus in the heart of the hills; he had beheld the stately tomb of the same hero on Mount Sipylus, the ruined city at the bottom of the clear lake, the rock-hewn throne of Pelops crowning the dizzy peak that overhangs the cañon, and the dripping rock which popular fancy took for the bereaved Niobe weeping for her children.

narrativeBlocks.title: The sea that mourns a king
narrativeBlocks.body: The Aegean Sea is named for Aegeus — Theseus's father who threw himself from the rock watching black sails. Every voyage on it says his name.

narrativeBlocks.title: The sky full of heroes
narrativeBlocks.body: Perseus, Andromeda, Cassiopeia, Cepheus, and Pegasus are all still overhead — the entire Andromeda rescue is preserved as constellations, plus Hercules kneeling with his club, Orion the hunter, and the Hydra Perseus never fought.

narrativeBlocks.title: Cities that claim founders
narrativeBlocks.body: Mycenae carries Perseus's founding; Athens wears Theseus's civic myth in its stones (the Parthenon's sculptures show the Centauromachy he fought in); Thebes is shaped by Cadmus's dragon-teeth founding.

narrativeBlocks.title: Monsters in the map
narrativeBlocks.body: Geography absorbed the mythic: the Pillars of Hercules (Gibraltar) are where his tenth labour ended; the Bosporus is 'cow's crossing' for Io the cow-maiden; the Hellespont is 'Helle's sea' for the girl who fell off the golden ram.

narrativeBlocks.title: Why landscape-myth matters
narrativeBlocks.body: The myths didn't live in books — they lived in places. Sailing the Aegean or looking up at Pegasus keeps the stories physically present, which is how they survived a thousand years.
